title: Silas and the Silver Trowel
markdown:
Silas the deer managed the Whispering Greenhouse. Sunlight painted the glass; air smelled of damp earth and his special mood flowers. They blushed when praised, wilted at unkind words, exploded in colour when happiness bloomed. Rowan the crow, midnight feathers, found lost things: a needle, a key, a runaway squirrel.

“The Lumina Bloom Exhibition,” Silas murmured, polishing a petal of Joyful Jasmine. Tomorrow. His place depended on an old tarnished silver trowel, grandmother’s, with a unique feel for delicate potting. He feared the judges would find the emotional blooms silly. Whiskers quivered.

A crisp envelope, Lumina crest, landed on the potting bench. Rowan, mid-preen, cocked his head. “Urgent summons. Submission by dawn. The exhibition starts then.”

“Dawn! My trowel!” He wrung his hooves. Gone. Without it, the presentation was lost. Lumina Bloom did not tolerate lateness.

“Then Lumina City,” Rowan declared, puffing. “Without delay.”

Lumina City assaulted his senses. Sounds clattered, colours blazed. Carts rumbled, vendors bellowed, a thousand voices merged into a single inconsiderate hum. Silas, used to the greenhouse’s gentle rustles, felt a tremor in his knees. Too much. Too loud. He should have stayed among mood flowers that at least wilted honestly. They hurried toward the grand halls of the Lumina Portrait Parlor, the last place he remembered seeing the trowel; he had meant to polish it there, away from damp, and had then forgotten the away.

Velvet curtains muffled the roar. Dust and old perfume. Mr Sterling, stern photographer, adjusted a towering camera. “Seeking something?” Silas explained in a whisper. Embarrassment warmed his neck. Quiet efforts felt clumsy under scrutiny. The urge to flee to damp earth was almost overwhelming. Hooves rooted.

Rowan hopped a plush chair, scanning edges: dusty plates, a draped corner. “Silas. Look.” The Velvet Vignette: heavy cloth, antique books, a tarnished silver trowel resting as if it had always been art.

“My trowel.” Relieved, confused. “A peculiar place for a gardening tool.”

Sterling huffed. “It is art. The Essence of Neglect. It resonates.” Shrewd gleam. “If you must retrieve it, you agree to a portrait. To integrate the piece properly.”

Silas hesitated. Exposed under an unyielding lens: fur ruffled, antlers askew, the calm keeper image shattered. They would see the fluster. Velvet creaked. Metallic tang. Stillness. Dawn was close. He nodded, heart frantic.

He stood awkwardly among books, velvet clinging, trowel clutched. Spotlight burned. Click of the shutter through his bones. Then over. He paid a sum that stung his savings. Privacy was the cost, the brief light burning away self-protection. The trowel felt warmer.

They raced back. Dawn painted the sky as Silas set the gleaming tool beside his mood flowers. The exhibition was a blur of hushed admiration. Blooms pulsed with inner light. The trowel sat beside them, silent testament.

Later, sunlight made dust into tiny fairies. A child pointed. “Look, Mama. The prettiest thing here. It looks like it holds secrets.”

Warmth richer than any joy he had coaxed from petals. He looked at the trowel, now holding Lumina, fear, and courage; at the flowers, thriving. Moonlight on stacked books in the greenhouse would keep a soft glow. His unfashionable ideas were not odd. They were his. The photographer’s light flickered in memory, and instead of fear a quiet confidence unfurled, a new bud in ordinary sun. He left the trowel on the bench unhidden, and Rowan, finding nothing lost for once, preened as if that, too, were a retrieval.
